Writing Documentation

On this page

Writing Published Feluqa Documentation ​

Use this workflow when creating or revising documentation intended for the Feluqa documentation site. The site is independent of Feluqa's private source tree. Write for the people who will read the published page, and preserve the product owner's meaning rather than turning it into a simpler but different idea.

Read the source material first ​

  1. Read the whole source document when the user names it as the basis for a page. Do not infer its thesis from one section or a search excerpt.
  2. Read Feluqa's canonical taxonomy and product intent. Check the relevant architecture and implementation-status documents before making claims about terms or capabilities. Consult local planning notes when available, but do not treat them as published product guarantees.
  3. Inspect the current documentation tree and nearby pages. Paths and numbering can change; do not assume a path from earlier conversation is still current.
  4. Keep a short map of which ideas belong in which pages before drafting. Use a concept page for one idea, a product page for a product proposal, and a reference page for detailed behavior. Do not compress several distinct ideas into a generic summary.

Preserve the owner's intent ​

  • Keep the owner's actual thesis and distinctions. Do not reduce an idea about extensible Modules, Features, hooks, agents, local execution, privacy, compilation, and distribution to a generic statement about small teams or automation.
  • When asked to remove one reference or phrase, make that narrow change and preserve the surrounding wording unless the user asks for a rewrite.
  • Do not introduce analogies, competitors, authors, or claims the user has rejected. In particular, do not add a monopoly framing or a reference to Peter Thiel or Zero to One when writing Feluqa's own strategy.
  • Retain the reader's agency. Prefer "your Product" or "your Application" when the reader may be a founder, company, CTO, developer, contractor, student, operator, or customer. Do not assume every reader personally wrote the software.
  • If a commercial, licensing, or ownership promise is ambiguous, clarify it before publishing a commitment. Distinguish "free of charge" from freedom to use, modify, contribute, or distribute.

Use the canonical taxonomy ​

Read Feluqa's Taxonomy before introducing or changing a domain term. In particular, keep these boundaries clear:

  • A Product is the business solution offered to an organisation or user.
  • An Application is a deployable program for an execution role.
  • A Module is a reusable unit of business capability included in an Application; a Feature is an optional capability within a Module or Application.
  • The Feluqa SDK is the development API and tooling. The Feluqa Platform is the runtime and control plane. Do not use either term as a synonym for a customer Product.
  • A crate is a Rust compilation unit; a package is a Cargo package; a workspace contains related packages and projects.

Avoid vague references such as "the repository" when they could mean the private Feluqa source tree, a product workspace, a Cargo package, a crate, a source distribution, or a customer's code. Name the exact thing.

Keep site documentation independent of private source files ​

Published docs must make sense to someone who has never seen Feluqa's private source tree. Do not link to local files such as LICENSE.md, README.md, or README_Product_Document_Intent.en.md with relative filesystem paths. Summarise the relevant content in the guide and link to another published guide page, the public website, or a file distributed with the relevant source code.

Do not make an unavailable UI or CLI resource sound live. If a future System Control Panel resource, public issue tracker, agent companion, or workflow is planned, say it is planned and explain the current path only if one exists.

Separate beliefs, targets, and delivered behavior ​

Use repository status documents and code to label claims accurately:

  • Delivered means implemented and supported in the current repository.
  • Target means an explicit product direction that is not yet a delivered guarantee.
  • Exploring means a hypothesis under evaluation.

The product intent document is normative for product direction, but it does not make a Target feature current. Do not present future dynamic Modules, agent identities, local-agent orchestration, model-provider choice, hooks, compile/package/distribute flows, or a companion project as implemented unless the current status documentation confirms it. Use "is intended to", "is a target", or "is planned" where appropriate.

Avoid unsupported percentages, performance claims, security guarantees, or claims that proprietary or open-source licensing by itself makes software secure. For technical security claims, use accurate wording and link to authoritative references.

Explain licensing and AI choices without conflating them ​

  • Proprietary describes ownership and distribution; it does not by itself mean no participation, no contributions, or no right to create Products.
  • State the owner's explicit guarantee about free Application creation and Product use before explaining framework ownership or optional services.
  • Keep the rights to the Feluqa SDK and Platform distinct from rights to a customer Product, its Applications and Modules, and customer-specific source.
  • If selective open-source releases are part of the stated direction, say which parts are confirmed and which crate-level decisions remain open. Do not imply every crate will be published.
  • Feluqa is intended to support local agents and agents selected by the user. Explain that the local path can keep business-specific context in the organisation's controlled environment; do not promise that a remote agent will keep data private. Describe the complementary agent project as separate and planned until it exists.
  • Do not imply agents can inject uncompiled code into a live application. Describe the intended workflow through explicit hooks/contracts, CLI inspection, generation, compilation, validation, testing, packaging, and controlled distribution; state which steps are not implemented yet.

When the content is a service offer, keep it in a clearly labelled section after the reader-facing product and licensing explanation. Do not turn a licensing introduction into an unexpected sales pitch.

Voice, tone, and reader fit ​

Write for people first. Keep paragraphs short and focused, use headings and lists to make long pages easy to scan, and add a diagram when it explains a relationship more clearly than prose. Use a conversational, friendly, and respectful voice: knowledgeable and natural, without slang, forced humor, overfamiliarity, or a formal legalistic tone. Make the information useful to a reader who may be in a hurry.

Write clearly for readers across languages and experience levels ​

  • Prefer familiar, precise words, active voice, and present tense. Put the person or thing doing the action near the beginning of the sentence. Address the reader directly as "you" when they perform the task; do not call them "the user" in instructions.
  • Keep one main idea in each sentence. Prefer short sentences; fewer than 26 words is a useful target, not a rigid limit. Avoid double negatives, exceptions to exceptions, unnecessary negative instructions, and unnecessary background that obscures what the reader needs to do.
  • Use standard English word order, clear conditional clauses, and parallel structure in lists. Keep technical terms, names, capitalization, dates, units, formatting, and repeated phrases consistent throughout the page and across related pages. Repeat a word when that removes ambiguity.
  • Choose simple verbs over formal or multiword phrases when their meaning is the same. Avoid phrasal verbs when a clear single verb works. Avoid vague modifiers such as "simply," "easy," "quickly," "properly," and "carefully"; state the actual result or action. Place modifiers such as "only" next to the words they qualify, and avoid long strings of noun modifiers.
  • Keep the main subject and verb close to the beginning. Avoid ambiguous use of participles such as "using" when a reader could mistake which action or noun they describe. Use words in their primary sense, and avoid directional references such as "above," "below," or "on the right" when a section name, label, or sequence number is clearer.
  • Write with translation and localization in mind. Localization can require adapting examples, units, dates, times, currencies, and interface language for a place; translation changes language; internationalization reduces the work needed to localize a product. Use unambiguous dates and measurements and avoid culturally specific jokes, holidays, sports, seasons, idioms, slang, and humor that may not travel well.

Use terminology readers can understand ​

  • Prefer plain, specific words to group-specific jargon, vague labels, or overloaded words such as "solution," "support," or "workload." Keep established technical terms when readers need them to find or understand a feature. Define an unfamiliar term at first use, or link to a trusted definition, and keep its meaning consistent.
  • If a term is used once, explain it in plain language and include the specialist term in parentheses only when readers benefit from knowing it. If it recurs, define it on first use. For command names and code identifiers, use code formatting and make clear which literal item you mean.
  • Use an abbreviation only when it helps the intended reader. Spell out an unfamiliar abbreviation at first use and add the abbreviation in parentheses. Avoid abbreviations unrelated to the page's subject and those used only once without benefit. Do not use "e.g.," "i.e.," internet shorthand such as "tl;dr" or "ymmv," or shortened forms when the full word is clearer. Follow standard spellings for technical names and file formats; don't alter code or interface labels to fit prose style.

Write inclusively and describe people respectfully ​

  • Use gender-neutral language when gender is irrelevant. Choose a diverse set of names, places, ages, and backgrounds in examples, and avoid assuming that every reader shares one culture, language, or experience.
  • Avoid wording that divides or stereotypes people, including unnecessary references to "native" and "non-native" language ability. Avoid ableist, violent, graphic, or demeaning expressions when a precise alternative works. Do not describe nondisabled people as "normal" or define a person only by a disability. Follow the terminology preferred by the community being discussed; preferences differ, so check rather than assume.
  • When an existing product identifier or code keyword uses a term that should not be repeated in prose, mention it only when necessary, format it as code, explain the preferred term, and use that term afterward. Preserve literal identifiers when documenting the code accurately.
  • Avoid metaphors and figures of speech, including familiar engineering metaphors. They can distract, obscure technical meaning, exclude readers, or translate unpredictably. Use the precise technical name; if an established term has no accurate substitute, define it once and minimize repetition.

Make documents accessible and easy to navigate ​

  • Break up dense text with focused paragraphs, descriptive headings, and lists. Use a logical heading hierarchy without skipped levels. Put the key point near the start of a paragraph, use consistent list grammar, and avoid hard line breaks inside prose paragraphs.
  • Write link text that explains the destination when read on its own. Avoid "click here" and "read this." Introduce interactive elements before the instructions for using them. Refer to controls by their visible labels, not by color, shape, position, or an icon alone; explain unexpected link actions.
  • Prefer prose or a list to a table when that is clearer. Introduce a table before it appears, use clear headings, and do not merge cells. Do not put essential information only in an image, color, position, or formatting. Provide equivalent text for diagrams and screenshots; give informative images useful alternative text and decorative images empty alternative text. Use actual text for code, terminal output, and text that readers must search or copy.
  • For web documentation, prefer semantic HTML and native controls. Make every control keyboard reachable and labelled. Keep DOM and visual reading order aligned, ensure adequate color contrast, do not hide content from assistive technology, and do not depend on hover alone. Provide captions, transcripts, or descriptions for audio and video, and avoid flashing content.
  • Check whether the page still communicates without color, images, sound, punctuation, or a mouse, and with magnified text. When practical, inspect rendered pages with keyboard navigation and a screen reader. Document product accessibility features and explain how to use them.

Use punctuation with restraint ​

  • End complete sentences with periods; do not put periods at the end of headings. Avoid exclamation points in reference and concept pages and usually in procedures. Tutorials may use one sparingly to mark a genuine milestone. System messages and code examples can retain punctuation required by their exact literal text or syntax.
  • Keep punctuation from carrying meaning that disappears for screen-reader users. Avoid unnecessary question marks, semicolons, ampersands in prose or headings, and punctuation inside acronyms. Keep one space between sentences. When a URL appears in prose, make it clear that a following period is not part of the address.

These are Feluqa's writing defaults. They do not override the canonical taxonomy, accurate technical names, the owner's meaning, or a specific user instruction. Follow narrow edits narrowly. If a general style rule conflicts with clarity for a particular audience, choose the clearer wording and keep the terminology consistent.

Structure and file naming ​

  • Keep one concept per Markdown file in the relevant concepts section; keep agent extensibility in 010-get-started/030-agentic-development/. Use a descriptive, topic-specific filename such as 000-agent-ready-extensible-modules.en.md.
  • Choose filenames and page titles that remain distinct across the whole future site. Avoid generic repeated names such as overview, concepts, or getting-started when a more specific slug is available.
  • The .en.md suffix identifies English. Do not repeat it with lang: en in front matter.
  • Include the required icon field and follow nearby front-matter structure.
  • Use an ordered folder structure consistently; add an Upgrade Guide only when a prior major version exists to upgrade from.

Final review ​

Before finishing:

  1. Compare the page against the owner's source text and confirm the core idea has not been flattened, contradicted, or expanded into an unapproved promise.

  2. Check Product, Application, Module, Feature, SDK, Platform, and CLI usage against the Taxonomy.

  3. Verify implementation-status statements against the current repository guidance. Treat unknown or incomplete behavior as unknown or incomplete.

  4. Check every local link from the page's actual location. Do not rely on local source-tree links for a published site.

  5. Run git diff --check. For documentation-only changes, review links, terminology, front matter, and rendering structure; do not run a runtime test suite unless requested or required by repository guidance.

  6. Apply the Feluqa voice and tone and the global-writing guidance above. Check that the prose stays concise, approachable, inclusive, and precise without changing the author's intended point.
